results.summary: This project implements a 12-bit digital-to-analog converter that produces a PWM output from a digital input. It is controlled by an external ESP32-WROOM-S3, which supplies clock, reset, enable, and the 12 input bits across the ui and uio pins. Testing involves driving the inputs with values such as 1024, 2048, and 4095 and observing the resulting PWM waveform on a wave analyzer or through the ESP32's serial output. The documentation is very brief, consisting of only a single sentence describing the design, so details of the internal implementation are not available.

This design is an 8-bit R-2R ladder digital-to-analog converter that can be driven either by external digital inputs or by an internal digitally generated sine waveform generator. It provides a 3.3 V analog output on a single analog pin, achieved through level-shifting drivers. The converter is tested by measuring the output voltage on the analog pin with a multimeter. The documentation is short but describes the core function and testing method clearly.

This project implements a digitally controlled oscillator that generates a frequency-adjustable clock signal from an 8-bit control input. The control input selects an oscillation period between 3 and 50 clock cycles using a priority-based scheme, with the highest active bit determining the period. A testbench is provided that simulates various input scenarios and monitors the output, with a table showing output frequencies ranging from 20 MHz down to 2.27 MHz for different input codes. The design is purely digital and requires no external hardware beyond the Tiny Tapeout board itself.

This design is a variable-delay chain intended for setup timing violation and glitching experiments. It contains eight delay chains, each with nine stages holding 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 96, and 128 inverter pairs, selectable via a test control input. Measurements require a carefully controlled glitchy clock, such as one generated by a ChipWhisperer, to arm and measure the delay line and observe setup violations. The module is aimed at evaluating the impact of place-and-route, temperature, and voltage on timing violations.

This project is a fully differential two-stage operational amplifier using a folded cascode followed by a common source stage. It has analog inputs for the differential signal, analog outputs for the differential output, a common-mode input pin, and two digital inputs to select between self-bias and external current source biasing. Testing is planned with an AD03 board to build a band-pass filter and measure linearity, offset voltage and current, CMRR, and PSRR. The design requires either a resistor for self-bias or an external current source, depending on the chosen biasing method.

This project is a digital playground that selects and tests eight classic digital blocks on a single Tiny Tapeout tile: logic gates, an 8-bit counter, a PWM generator, a 7-segment display driver, a 4-bit ALU, a frequency-to-digital converter, a 16x4 RAM, and turn-signal indicators. The active block is chosen with three mode-select inputs, and the remaining pins serve as block-specific inputs and outputs. Testing requires external hardware such as LEDs, switches, a 7-segment display, a function generator, and a logic analyzer or oscilloscope. The design is intended for education and experimentation, with all unused outputs forced to zero and bidirectional pins used only as inputs.

This project is a standalone TinyQV I2C controller device that also exposes SPI signals and interrupt outputs. The pin functions are configurable through a CMUX register, and testing may require an NPN transistor and external pull-up resistors on the I2C bus lines. The documentation is incomplete, with a TODO and vague testing instructions, so the exact behavior and configuration are not fully described. It is intended to interface with external I2C and SPI peripherals, possibly using an RP2040.

This project implements a simple Tiny DMA controller for memory-to-memory copy operations, supporting both single-word and three-word burst transfers. It uses a finite state machine with IDLE, TRANSFER, and DONE states, and produces a dma_done pulse when the transfer completes, outputting the last transferred data on uo_out. The design is verified with a Cocotb testbench that checks single and burst transfers, confirming values such as 0x61 and 0x63 appear on the output. The documentation is clear about the design and testing, though the clock is specified as 10 Hz, which is unusually low.

This project implements a Dynamic Power Management Unit for a System on Chip in SystemVerilog. It dynamically adjusts voltage and frequency levels based on inputs such as performance requirements, temperature, battery level, and workload, using a finite state machine to manage transitions between power states. The documentation is very brief and does not describe the pin functions or testing procedure in detail. No external hardware or specific test setup is mentioned.

This project is a streaming arbitrary waveform generator that outputs 8-bit digital samples on eight output pins, which must be connected to an external R-2R ladder or similar DAC to produce an analog waveform. Waveform data is loaded via SPI into a shift register and then transferred to an active register when the load signal is asserted, allowing data to be changed while streaming. The output frequency is derived from the clock with optional dividers of 2x, 4x, 16x, and 256x, which can be stacked for up to 32768x division. Testing requires an external microcontroller to provide SPI data and a DAC circuit to convert the digital outputs to analog.
